svg.title: One token costs a 32.8 GB read and 65.6 GFLOP
svg.desc: The roofline argument for a 32B model on an H100, with the arithmetic shown. Every token re-reads all 32.8 GB of weights and computes only 65.6 GFLOP with them — 2.00 FLOP per byte against a chip that needs 295 FLOP per byte to keep its units fed, so 1 of 132 SMs has work. Batching 18 sequences shares one read and lifts that to 36.0 FLOP per byte; a 19th sequence needs 2.00 GiB of KV cache that does not exist.
svg.text: One token costs a 32.8 GB read and 65.6 GFLOP
Read the numbers, not the shapes — every quantity here is a solve, and the arithmetic that produced it is printed beside it
Qwen3-32B · 32.8B params · q8 (8 bits per weight) · 8,192-token context · NVIDIA H100 80 GB SXM · 72.0 GiB usable after runtime overhead
all 32.8 GB again, for every token
= 73.5 tokens/s — bandwidth estimate, not a measurement
at one sequence at a time.
Why 131 engines idle: the machine reads far more than it computes
989.4 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s — where the two break even
where that intensity sits, log scale
Batching is the lever — and the KV cache is where it stops
KV cache = the attention keys and values each sequence keeps for its own context; every concurrent sequence needs its own copy
the read is spent on one token
1.51 GiB spare — the last batch that fits
0.49 GiB over — the 19th needs 2.00 GiB of KV
The ceiling is memory, not maths: 18 sequences share one 32.8 GB read and reach 36.0 FLOP/byte — still 8× under the 295 the chip needs — and
the batch stops at 18 because KV cache ran out, not compute. Shrinking that cache (lighter quantisation, shorter context, an MLA model) buys
batch, and batch is the only thing that buys intensity. Figures are a real `clickllm fit` solve; 73.5 tokens/s is a bandwidth estimate, not
